title: StoryboardClear
question: How do screenplays and storyboards work?
hook: Before a camera rolls, a film already exists twice: as a script where one page is about one minute, and as a comic strip of every shot. Write a scene, board it from a 3D camera, cross the 180-degree line and play your own animatic.

explainer.title: A script is a timed blueprint
explainer.text: Screenplays use 12-point Courier and fixed margins for headings, action, names and dialogue, so one page runs about one minute. A 110-page script makes a film of roughly two hours.

explainer.title: Stories have a shape
explainer.text: Most films follow three acts: set-up, confrontation, resolution, with turning points that push the tension up to a climax. Indian films add an interval, with a big twist just before it.

explainer.title: Words become pictures
explainer.text: A storyboard draws every shot. Each one picks a shot size, from extreme wide to extreme close-up, an angle such as low, high or Dutch, and a move such as a pan, tilt, dolly or track.

explainer.title: Coverage and the line
explainer.text: A scene is filmed from several set-ups: a master, over-the-shoulders and close-ups. Keep every camera on one side of the line between two characters, or they swap sides on screen.

explainer.title: Timing before shooting
explainer.text: An animatic plays the panels in time with temp sound. Pre-vis rebuilds the scene in simple 3D, as big action films like Baahubali and RRR did, so costly shots are solved on a computer first.

explainer.title: You direct
explainer.text: Board a six-shot scene yourself. A checklist catches the classic mistakes: no establishing shot, jump cuts, a crossed line, no close-up, or a scene that runs far longer than its page count.

concepts.def: A film script in a standard layout: 12-point Courier, fixed margins, roughly one page per minute of screen time.
The line that opens a scene: INT. or EXT., the place and the time of day, such as EXT. ROOFTOP - DAY.
Set-up, confrontation and resolution, split roughly a quarter, a half and a quarter of the script.
A sequence of drawings, one per shot, showing what the camera will see.
How much of the subject fills the frame: extreme wide, wide, medium, close-up or extreme close-up.
Filming one scene from several set-ups, such as a master, over-the-shoulders and close-ups, so the editor has choices.
Keep the camera on one side of the line between two characters so each stays on the same side of the screen.
Storyboard panels cut together in time with rough sound, to test a scene's rhythm.
Previsualisation: planning shots with a simple 3D model of the set, actors and cameras before shooting.

storage.what: Which chapters you have opened, your best quiz scores, and sound on or off.
